Author: Yolanda Berdugo
BRUSHING

Much of the Shih Tzu's elegance comes from its beautiful coat. Maintaining that elegance requires careful brushing. This takes around 15 minutes a day and can be an enjoyable time for both you and your dog.

You will need the following equipment: a soft brush; a large comb, useful for the head rather than the body; a small facial comb to remove any build-up around the eyes; a hairdryer; scissors measuring 10 to 12 cm. for trimming the hair around the paws; and a spray bottle containing one part grooming conditioner to eight parts water, to mist the coat as you brush.
Begin by gently brushing all the hair backwards, without dragging or pulling hard. The aim is simply to move the hair back before starting the thorough brushing.

Brush section by section, starting at the front of the dog and paying particular attention to the belly and front legs. Work through a small amount of hair at a time until the whole section is thoroughly brushed. Each section should be 10 cm. wide. Once one section is finished, move on to the next, continuing until you reach the hind legs.
Take particular care around the eyes and moustache. Use a small comb as slowly and gently as possible to remove any build-up around the eyes, which could otherwise cause discomfort or injury.

Once the face is groomed, make the topknots. Section the hair from approximately the centre of each eye, following a line upwards to the middle of the head. Divide the hair at the centre of the head, making sure the sections are even on both sides. Hold the gathered hair in one hand and use the other to secure it with a small latex band, taking care not to catch or tangle any hairs in the band. Once secured, comb the topknot so that the hair falls to either side.

BATHING
Before bathing, there are a few things to remember. Brush your dog thoroughly before washing. Any knots or tangles left in the coat will be twice as difficult to comb out afterwards.
A drop of mineral oil in each eye before bathing helps reduce problems caused by soap getting into the eyes. Keep the drain open while washing your dog. The water should be lukewarm, not hot.

Put shampoo into your hands and apply it directly to your dog's coat. Work it through from roots to tips with a gentle kneading motion. If your dog is dirty or has not been bathed for some time, a second shampoo will probably be needed. After rinsing out all the shampoo, apply a conditioner mixed with a little water to make the coat more manageable and add shine.

Before lifting your dog out of the bath, gently squeeze the excess water from the coat. Wrap your dog in a towel and take them to the drying area. Blot the coat with a towel without rubbing, and allow a few shakes to help speed up drying. Dry the coat in sections with a hairdryer, starting with the belly. Brush each area as you direct the airflow onto it. Once your dog is dry, brush the entire coat again to make sure there are no tangles. The bathing process takes around 40 minutes, depending on the coat's thickness and length.

EARS, TEETH AND NAILS

The ears should be free of hair to help prevent infections and hearing loss. Do not trim the hair yourself unless you know how to do so properly. Ask your breeder or vet for guidance. All hair inside the ear should be removed with tweezers, never cut.

Brushing your dog's teeth is beneficial. There are several ways to do it, and the best approach depends on what works for you and your dog. Some dogs dislike having something put in their mouths. Be gentle and speak reassuringly. Ask your vet for advice on maintaining good dental hygiene.

Your dog's nails should be trimmed weekly, especially if they do not wear down naturally. If allowed to grow too long, they can cause the toes to splay and affect posture. Trim carefully to avoid the "quick", the pink, living part of the nail. If accidentally cut, it will bleed. The quick is visible as a pink area in white nails, but with dark nails you must trim only a very small amount at a time. Trimming the tips every week makes the task much easier.
